prior_decision.reason: The paper explicitly cites Kuziemko et al. (2013) for the flat or decreasing U.S. trend in redistribution demand that it documents and replicates in Section I.A, making it a valid omitted target.

luna_triage.reason: This paper directly re-tests the previously reported aggregate trend of flat or declining U.S. demand for redistribution using its survey measures and datasets. The reference identifies Kuziemko et al. 2013 as “How Elastic Are Preferences for Redistribution? Evidence from Randomized Survey Experiments.” The supplied shipped row is Kenworthy and McCall’s distinct 2007 online-first/2008 print paper, which the prior adjudication confirms is a separate target; it does not represent the Kuziemko work.
luna_triage.location: Introduction p. 368; Section I and I.A; references p. 404
luna_triage.omission_quote: In the first part of the paper, we replicate past work, showing that trends in the demand for redistribution among Americans has been largely flat or perhaps slightly negative over the last four decades.
luna_triage.identity_quote: Kuziemko, Ilyana, Michael I. Norton, Emmanuel Saez, and Stefanie Stantcheva. 2013. “How Elastic Are Preferences for Redistribution? Evidence from Randomized Survey Experiments.”
luna_triage.duplicate_quote: Beyond the United States, citizens of other countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) that have seen rising income inequality generally have not exhibited greater demand for redistribution (Kenworthy and McCall 2008).
